clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia mapped to chromosome 10q22.1-q24.1, originally described in a French-Canadian family and in consanguineous kindreds.
Presents as either a pure or a complicated phenotype; the complicated form includes intellectual disability, a sensory axonal neuropathy, dysarthria and mild cerebellar signs.
Dysmorphic features, short stature and microcephaly have been reported in some families, broadening the recognised phenotype.
Age at onset is variable, ranging from childhood to adulthood.
A sensory axonal neuropathy on nerve conduction studies is a useful discriminating pointer within the recessive HSP differential.
The causative gene has not yet been confirmed, so diagnosis relies on the phenotype together with locus linkage or exclusion.
Consider it alongside SPG24 and SPG28 among the early-onset autosomal recessive complicated HSPs.
Management is symptomatic only, with no disease-modifying therapy available.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG27 is an autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia linked to chromosome 10q22.1-q24.1, mapped in a French-Canadian family and subsequently in consanguineous kindreds. As throughout the HSP group, the central lesion is a length-dependent, retrograde degeneration of the longest corticospinal tract axons producing progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness, but in SPG27 there is additional involvement of the peripheral sensory axons, giving the sensory axonal neuropathy that characterises the complicated form. The multisystem features reported in some families, including intellectual disability, cerebellar signs, dysmorphism, short stature and microcephaly, imply that the underlying defect extends beyond the corticospinal system to broader neurodevelopment. The single causative gene at the SPG27 locus has not been identified, so the molecular mechanism remains unproven; by analogy with other recessive HSPs it is presumed to disturb a fundamental neuronal maintenance process such as axonal transport, lipid or membrane handling, or mitochondrial function.
additionalDifferentials: SPG24 and SPG28 - sibling autosomal recessive early-onset subtypes
SPG7 (paraplegin) - recessive HSP often with cerebellar or ocular features
SPG11 (spatacsin) - recessive HSP with a thin corpus callosum and cognitive decline
SPG15 (ZFYVE26, Kjellin syndrome) - complicated HSP with retinopathy, thin corpus callosum and cognitive impairment
SPG16 - X-linked complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia
Hereditary sensory and motor neuropathies - given the accompanying sensory neuropathy
Metabolic mimics such as arginase deficiency and dopa-responsive dystonia
additionalInvestigations: MRI of brain and spinal cord, assessing for a thin corpus callosum, cerebellar atrophy and structural or demyelinating disease
Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to characterise the sensory axonal neuropathy
Next-generation sequencing HSP gene panels and autozygosity mapping in consanguineous families
Neuropsychological evaluation where cognitive impairment is suspected
Ophthalmological assessment including the retina to exclude the retinopathy of Kjellin syndrome
Metabolic screen including very-long-chain fatty acids and plasma amino acids
Growth and dysmorphology assessment where short stature or microcephaly is present
redFlags: Rapid progression or a sensory level suggesting a compressive or structural cord lesion
Retinal changes suggesting an alternative complicated HSP such as Kjellin syndrome
Rapid cognitive decline suggesting a broader neurodegenerative disorder
Systemic or metabolic features suggesting an inborn error of metabolism
reference.prognosis: The disorder is slowly progressive, and ambulation is variably preserved depending on the phenotype. Complicated features such as cognitive impairment and neuropathy increase overall disability, and no curative treatment exists.
pitfalls: Assuming a pure HSP and omitting nerve conduction studies, thereby missing the associated sensory neuropathy
Interpreting a negative single-gene test as excluding SPG27, since the gene is unconfirmed
Overlooking overlap with SPG11 and SPG15, which do have specific genetic tests
Allowing dysmorphic features to divert the work-up towards an unrelated syndromic diagnosis
references: Neurogenetics reference literature on hereditary spastic paraplegia
Hereditary spastic paraplegia classification and review articles
management: No gene-directed therapy exists; manage lower-limb spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses and walking aids to maintain ambulation and prevent contractures
Educational and neuropsychological support for the associated intellectual disability
Speech and language therapy for dysarthria, with podiatry and orthotic support for the sensory axonal neuropathy
Monitor growth and development given short stature and microcephaly, with paediatric input
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with carrier testing and consanguinity-related recurrence-risk discussion
Escalate to multidisciplinary rehabilitation as disability accrues
